# Abstract

The lower Mekong basin, the Tonle Sap lacustrine depression and the narrow littoral plains of central and southern Vietnam encompass 243.324 km² of tropical riverine, wetland and coastal terrain. Spanning 3.018 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells, this macro-region supported one of the most sophisticated low-density agrarian civilisations in world history. Between 500BC and 1862AD, successive socio-political formations—the proto-historic maritime realm of Funan, the inland riverine polities of Chenla, the Cham principalities of the Annamite littoral and the unified hydraulic empire of Angkor—transformed wild floodplains into engineered agrarian landscapes capable of supporting dense human populations.

Reconstructed across four physiographic divisions under MANDALA, aggregate population grew from 1,1M inhabitants in 500BC during the late Iron Age to 1,75M in 200AD as maritime trade corridors through Oc Eo stimulated urban nucleation. Population expanded to 2,3M in 700AD during the Chenla period and attained 2,95M in 1000AD under early Angkorian expansion. The regional demographic apex occurred in 1200AD during the reign of Jayavarman VII, when total population reached 3,6M inhabitants (an aggregate regional density of 1.479,51 persons per 100 km²). Following fourteenth-century hydroclimatic volatility, regional conflicts and administrative restructuring, demographic mass contracted to 2,4M in 1431AD, 1,55M in 1600AD, 1,3M in 1800AD and 1,15M in 1862AD upon the establishment of French colonial administration.

Demographic mass remained heavily focused within the alluvial and lacustrine lowlands. At the 1200AD climax, the Tonle Sap and Angkor hydraulic basin accommodated 1,37M people (38% of regional population; 1.634,82 persons per 100 km²), anchored by the sprawling low-density metropolis of Greater Angkor. The Lower Mekong and Angkor Borei-Chaktomuk core supported 1,01M inhabitants (28%; 2.521,2 persons per 100 km²), while the Champa maritime corridor accommodated 792k people (22%; 1.561,85 persons per 100 km²) distributed across estuarine valleys from Amaravati to Panduranga. The Cardamom coast and upper Mekong uplands housed 432k individuals (12%; 626,5 persons per 100 km²), sustaining forest gathering and swidden cultivation.

This demographic synthesis reconciles 156 catalogued settlements with multi-sensor airborne LiDAR micro-topography, archaeological surveys, epigraphic inventories and palaeoclimate records. By subtracting nucleated civic and ceremonial centres from rural cultivators dasymetrically mapped across alluvial soils, the reconstruction demonstrates that the fourteenth-century transformation of Angkor represented an adaptive geographic reorientation toward maritime trade nodes in the Mekong delta rather than wholesale demographic collapse.

# Background

## Fluvial Ecology and Monsoon Dynamics

The physical environment of mainland South-East Asia is governed by the regime of the Asian monsoon and the hydrological rhythm of the Mekong River [@Marko2020Historical]. Originating in the high Tibetan plateau, the Mekong traverses more than 4.000 km before entering the Cambodian lowlands. The river carries substantial seasonal discharges that expand downstream floodplains during the summer monsoon between June and November, when maritime air masses deliver intense precipitation across the catchment. Below the confluence at Chaktomuk, the river divides into the Mekong proper and the Bassac distributary, depositing mineral-rich alluvium across the deltaic plain before discharging into the South China Sea.

The defining hydrological feature of the interior basin is the Tonle Sap lake, connected to the Mekong trunk stream by the 100 km long Tonle Sap River. During the peak summer inundation, floodwaters from the Mekong reverse the flow of the Tonle Sap River, expanding the surface area of the lake from approximately 2.500 km² during the dry season to over 12.000 km² at the height of the flood. This annual flood-pulse deposits fine volcanic-derived sediments across extensive lacustrine plains, sustains an exceptionally productive freshwater fishery and creates extensive natural wetlands suited to recession rice cultivation [@Marko2020Historical].

The seasonal expansion of the Tonle Sap lake operates through a critical hydrological threshold. As the Mekong flood crest passes Kompong Cham, water levels rise to over 9 metres above dry-season baselines, overwhelming the natural hydraulic gradient and forcing water backward into the lake. This hydrodynamic inversion traps suspended sediment loads, depositing fertile alluvial silts across more than 10.000 km² of floodplain forests and backswamp depressions.

These seasonal inundations trigger massive reproductive migrations of freshwater fish species, predominantly cyprinids (*Henicorhynchus*) and silurids (*Pangasius*). The annual flood recession concentrated millions of fish into narrow distributary channels where local populations deployed bamboo barrages and lift-nets, securing animal protein reserves that sustained high human population densities throughout the dry season.

East of the Mekong basin, the Annamite Range forms a formidable topographical barrier separating the interior lowlands from the coastal plains of central Vietnam. Here, narrow river valleys debouch into coastal embayments, creating discrete agricultural pockets separated by rocky headlands and promontories. These coastal plains receive seasonal moisture from the northeast winter monsoon as well as summer typhoons, creating microclimatic regimes distinct from the interior monsoonal rhythms of the Tonle Sap basin.

South and southwest of the central basin, the Cardamom and Elephant mountain ranges capture heavy orographic rainfall, exceeding 4.000 mm annually along coastal slopes. These forested uplands provided timber, aromatic resins, cardamom and mineral ores that fed downstream trade circuits along the Gulf of Thailand and the lower Mekong.

## Proto-Historic Agrarian Systems: Funan and Early Maritime Networks

Prior to the consolidation of centralised territorial states, the lower Mekong delta supported late prehistoric and early historic societies engaged in wetland agriculture and maritime trade. Known to third-century Chinese chroniclers as Funan, this polity occupied the estuarine floodplains and mangrove fringes of southern Cambodia and the Transbassac region [@Owen2022Small].

Archaeological excavations at Oc Eo in An Giang province and Angkor Borei in Takeo province have documented extensive networks of engineered canals cut through deltaic alluvium, functioning concurrently as transport arteries, agricultural drainage channels and municipal water conduits [@Owen2022Small]. These settlements engaged in extensive international commerce connecting Han China, India and the eastern Roman Empire, as evidenced by imported Roman antoniniani, gold medallions, glass beads and inscribed seals.

Aerial surveys and ground investigations across the Transbassac have revealed that the canal network around Oc Eo extended over 200 km, connecting coastal anchorages with inland river distributaries. These linear watercourses served as conduits for communication, freshwater distribution and seasonal sediment flushing. Residential clusters along these canals were constructed on artificial earthen platforms elevated above annual flood marks, establishing an architectural template of earthen mound dwelling that persisted throughout the historical era.

The material culture of Funan reflects profound cosmopolitan engagement with Indian Ocean trade circuits. Excavations have yielded Roman medallions of Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius, gold repousse jewellery, carnelian intaglios engraved with classical Hellenistic and Indian deities and Sanskrit inscriptions in southern Brahmi script. These luxury goods circulated within elite administrative echelons, legitimising political authority and coordinating regional agrarian production.

Excavations at late prehistoric mortuary sites such as Prohear in Prey Veng province and Phum Snay in Banteay Meanchey demonstrate that late Iron Age communities possessed sophisticated metallurgy, working high-tin bronze and iron into weaponry, personal ornaments and agricultural implements. These burial assemblages indicate emerging social stratification and territorial polities during the final centuries BC, establishing the demographic foundations upon which Funan later expanded.

Agrarian production in this estuarine environment combined floating rice (*Oryza sativa*) adapted to seasonal water rises with estuarine fisheries, turtle harvesting and coastal foraging. Settlement systems consisted of moated circular and sub-rectangular enclosures elevated on natural levee mounds above annual flood levels. These proto-historic communities laid the technical foundations for hydraulic management that subsequent inland states expanded across the interior floodplains.

## The Chenla Polities and Inland Agrarian Reorientation

Between the sixth and eighth centuries AD, the political and demographic centre of gravity shifted upstream from the coastal delta into the middle Mekong and Tonle Sap basins. Chinese historical records distinguish between Water Chenla in the southern delta and Land Chenla in the interior uplands, though archaeological evidence demonstrates a mosaic of autonomous, competing chiefdoms rather than centralised states.

Inland polities developed sophisticated bunded field networks and seasonal storage tanks, reducing reliance on natural estuarine flooding. Early urban centres such as Isanapura (Sambor Prei Kuk) along the Sen River and Bhavapura along the upper Mekong exhibited brick temple complexes, earthen ramparts and hydraulic reservoirs. Excavations at Sambor Prei Kuk demonstrate that urban occupation was structured around octagonal and rectangular brick sanctuaries, water storage basins (*trapeang*) and earthen causeways accommodating administrative personnel, artisans and religious officiants.

The transition from Funan to Chenla was characterised by ideological and spatial reconfiguration. Where Funan had looked outward toward maritime exchange corridors across the Gulf of Thailand, Chenla polities turned inland toward the fertile interfluves and piedmont zones of the middle Mekong and northern lacustrine plains. Here, political elites mobilised peasant labour to erect stone and brick temple complexes that functioned as cosmological anchors for regional agricultural communities.

Epigraphic records from the seventh and eighth centuries AD document the institutionalisation of the *asrama* and *devasthana* (temple foundation). Inscriptions at Sambor Prei Kuk record the donation of rice fields (*ksetra*), orchards, cattle and indentured personnel (*khnum*) to maintain daily rituals, temple offerings and priestly staff. These religious institutions acted as agrarian development corporations, clearing secondary forest, constructing earthen water reservoirs (*trapeang*) and organising communal hydraulic labour.

Along the middle Mekong, religious centres such as Vat Phu (Champasak) anchored sacred landscapes dedicated to Bhadresvara, coordinating agricultural labour across fertile riverine terraces. Further downstream, settlements such as Banteay Prei Nokor established monumental brick ramparts that presaged classical Khmer urban morphology.

Inscriptions written in Sanskrit and Old Khmer record donations of land, cattle and bound agricultural labourers to religious foundations, indicating the emergence of an institutionalised agrarian economy capable of supporting elite administrative hierarchies. These institutional developments facilitated the coordination of communal labour necessary for regional hydraulic engineering.

## The Classical Angkorian Hydraulic Empire and Demographic Apex

In 802AD, Jayavarman II established the Angkorian state near Mount Kulen, initiating four centuries of territorial expansion and architectural monumentalism. At the urban centre of Yasodharapura (Angkor), successive rulers constructed an integrated water-management apparatus spanning more than 1.000 km² [@Sarah2021Provisioni; @Terry2018Evidence].

The Angkorian hydraulic apparatus comprised four principal components:
1. Vast artificial reservoirs (*baray*), notably the East Baray (Yashodharatataka, capacity ca. 55M m³), the West Baray (capacity ca. 120M m³) and the Jayatataka, engineered with elevated earthen dykes rather than excavated basins.
2. An extensive network of primary and secondary canals that diverted seasonal runoff from the Kulen hills to fill reservoirs, irrigate bunded paddy fields and drain excess monsoon overflow into the Tonle Sap [@Terry2018Evidence].
3. Thousands of localised household and village ponds (*trapeang*) serving domestic water needs during the six-month dry season.
4. Linear transport causeways and dykes that doubled as flood-control barriers and communication routes across the wetland landscape [@Sarah2021Provisioni].

This hydraulic infrastructure insulated rice cultivation against seasonal droughts, permitting double and triple cropping across favoured sectors of the Tonle Sap plain. Under Suryavarman II (r. 1113-1150AD) and Jayavarman VII (r. 1181-1218AD), the empire achieved its maximum territorial reach, extending from the Mekong delta to the Khorat plateau and southern Laos [@Thomas2009Khmer; @Thun2026Khmer].

To coordinate administration across this imperial expanse, the state constructed monumental royal highways (*phlu luk*) lined with rest-houses (*dharmasala*) and medical hospitals (*arogyasala*). Massive laterite and sandstone corbelled bridges (*spean*), such as Spean Praptos near Kompong Kdei, spanned major rivers, facilitating trade and troop movements throughout the year.

Along these imperial routes, Jayavarman VII established a network of 121 rest-houses with fire (*dharmasala*) and 102 regional hospitals (*arogyasala*). Epigraphic stelae recovered from these hospital compounds record detailed inventories of medicinal supplies, medical staff and rice rations allocated to treat local populations and pilgrims. This state-sponsored infrastructure reduced mortality from endemic tropical diseases and facilitated demographic stability across provincial territories.

The physical footprint of Angkor was organised as a dispersed agro-urban complex. Rather than concentrating inhabitants within dense walled perimeters, the capital dispersed domestic dwellings across tens of thousands of bunded agricultural plots interspersed with residential mounds, communal shrines and water tanks. This spatial layout supported extraordinarily high regional carrying capacity while minimising epidemiological vulnerabilities common to densely congested pre-industrial walled cities [@Sarah2021Provisioni; @Asmita2021Challenges].

## Champa Maritime Principalities along the Annamite Littoral

Contemporaneous with the rise of Funan and Angkor, Austronesian-speaking Cham populations established a confederation of maritime principalities along the central and southern coast of Vietnam. Organized into regional domains—Amaravati in the north, Vijaya in Binh Dinh, Kauthara around Nha Trang and Panduranga in the south—Champa societies combined intensive wet-rice farming in coastal river deltas with long-distance maritime commerce and upland forest trade [@Mupiza2016Pengaruh].

Cham settlements were situated at the mouths of navigable rivers, anchored by fortified citadels such as Tra Kieu (Simhapura), Cha Ban (Vijaya) and Phan Rang (Panduranga). Religious architecture featured brick sanctuaries dedicated to Siva and regional ancestral deities, constructed at sites like My Son and Po Nagar. The Cham fleet dominated maritime trading routes across the South China Sea, exporting aromatic woods, eaglewood, camphor and sea products to Song China. Relations between Champa, the Khmer Empire and the Vietnamese kingdom of Dai Viet alternated between diplomatic alliances and protracted military campaigns, including the Khmer sacking of Vijaya in 1145AD and the Cham naval assault on Angkor in 1177AD [@Mupiza2016Pengaruh].

The political architecture of Champa was defined by regional autonomy and polycentric authority. Rather than a centralised unitary empire, Champa operated as a federation of river-mouth principalities bounded by mountain defiles. The northern principality of Amaravati was anchored by the religious sanctuary of My Son and the fortified river capital of Tra Kieu, dominating trade along the Thu Bon River. Further south, the principality of Vijaya commanded the fertile alluvial basin of Binh Dinh from its fortified citadel at Cha Ban, acting as the primary political capital of Champa from the eleventh to the fifteenth century.

In Kauthara (Khanh Hoa) and Panduranga (Ninh Thuan and Binh Thuan), Cham communities exploited coastal lagoons, salt pans and swift mountain streams. The temple complex of Po Nagar at Nha Trang served as the spiritual centre for southern Champa, where inscriptions record royal gifts of gold, silver, paddy fields and slave families to the goddess Yan Pu Nagara. These coastal polities maintained active maritime trade with Java, the Philippines and Song China, exporting aromatic woods and importing fine porcelain and silk.

In the agricultural valleys of Quang Nam and Binh Dinh, Cham communities developed complex earthen dykes and stone sluices to divert river runoff into terraced paddy fields. These coastal agricultural belts supported dense populations capable of sustaining maritime fleets and monumental temple construction over centuries.

# Methodology

## Remote Sensing, LiDAR Micro-Topography and Epigraphic Corroboration

Demographic reconstruction across forested tropical terrain requires non-destructive remote sensing combined with ground-truthed archaeological surveys [@S2018Automated; @Diaz2022Prospecci]. Airborne LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) surveys conducted across the Angkor World Heritage site, Phnom Kulen, Koh Ker, Banteay Chhmar and Sambor Prei Kuk have revolutionised understandings of Khmer settlement morphology [@Edisa2016Arheolo; @Maria2025Pholidalta]. By filtering vegetation canopy returns, LiDAR reveals an extensive, contiguous landscape of residential earthen mounds, field boundaries, occupational ponds and local roads extending far beyond monumental temple enclosures.

These micro-topographic earthworks confirm that Angkor was not an empty ceremonial centre, but a low-density urban sprawl housing hundreds of thousands of cultivators, artisans and administrative personnel [@Sarah2021Provisioni; @Asmita2021Challenges]. Complementing LiDAR data, high-resolution multispectral satellite imagery and historical aerial photography provide regional coverage across the lower Mekong and coastal Vietnam [@Dominik2024Traismaure]. Epigraphic records written in Sanskrit and Old Khmer provide vital demographic cross-checks, detailing the allocation of temple staff, village tax rolls, slave counts and agricultural yields [@Thomas2009Khmer].

Processing LiDAR data involves classifying point clouds to separate tree canopy reflections from ground elevation returns. Digital terrain models (DTMs) derived from bare-earth surfaces reveal subtle linear ridges, micro-canals and sunken reservoirs with vertical relief of less than 30 cm, features completely invisible under optical satellite imagery or dense vegetation cover [@Edisa2016Arheolo].

## Dasymetric Spatial Allocation and Settlement Subtraction

To prevent double counting and ensure methodological consistency, this study employs dasymetric spatial disaggregation combined with settlement subtraction. The total regional demographic estimate at each chronological benchmark is derived from regional agrarian carrying capacity, historical chronicles and comparative demography [@Sarah2021Provisioni].

Catalogued nucleated settlements are assigned empirical population trajectories based on enclosed urban area, residential mound counts and documented dwelling densities. These nucleated populations are then subtracted from the sub-regional total, leaving the residual rural population to be dasymetrically distributed across active terrestrial cells according to environmental suitability weights (including soil fertility, proximity to perennial waterways, elevation and slope). This approach preserves the distinct footprint of urban metropolises while accurately representing dispersed rural populations across the countryside.

The dasymetric disaggregation framework uses high-resolution multi-layer GIS models to allocate rural populations outside nucleated settlements. Active terrestrial 5-arcminute grid cells are assigned continuous suitability scores based on environmental predictors:
- Proximity to perennial rivers, lake shorelines and historical canal lines, calibrated using negative exponential distance-decay functions.
- Hydrological inundation regimes, distinguishing between high-yield recession floodplains and chronically waterlogged backswamps.
- Soil agricultural capability, favouring fertile fluvisols and gleysols while penalising infertile acrisols.
- Slope constraints, progressively reducing residential carrying capacity above 5 degrees slope.

By subtracting the enumerated populations of primary and secondary catalogued settlements from total sub-regional benchmarks, the residual rural population is mapped across cells in strict accordance with their calculated carrying capacities. This methodology prevents arbitrary spatial smearing and eliminates urban double counting.

## Agricultural Multi-Cropping and Caloric Calibration

Agrarian carrying capacity was modelled using historical rice yields, nutritional requirements and flood-plain ecology [@Sarah2021Provisioni; @Visotheary2023Project]. In the Tonle Sap basin, traditional wet-rice agriculture yields between 1,2 and 1,8 tonnes of paddy per hectare under single-crop rainfall regimes, rising to 2,5 to 3,5 tonnes per hectare in irrigated zones served by *baray* distribution networks.

Assuming an average per-capita caloric requirement of 2.100 kcal per day (equivalent to approximately 200 kg of milled rice annually), one square kilometre of cultivated wetland could support between 400 and 700 persons. The Tonle Sap fishery provided an indispensable source of animal protein, yielding over 200.000 tonnes of freshwater fish annually under historical conditions. This nutritional abundance permitted extraordinary population densities in the immediate vicinity of the lake without requiring unsustainable long-distance food transport [@Sarah2021Provisioni].

Caloric accounting also considers multi-tiered crop diversification, including flood-recession rice, floating rice, maize and tubers in post-Columbian eras, alongside household gardens producing coconuts, bananas, betel nut and vegetables. This dietary breadth supported resilient rural communities across periods of climatic volatility.

Labour mobilization models calibrate the demographic requirements for monumental earthwork construction against seasonal agricultural cycles. Constructing the West Baray, which involved moving approximately 12M m³ of earth to form elevated dykes, required an estimated 10.000 to 15.000 corvee workers active over multiple dry seasons. Because hydraulic maintenance could only occur during the dry months between December and May when floodwaters receded, state administration coordinated corvee drafts to avoid depleting the agricultural labour force during critical transplanting and harvesting windows.

## Source Ledger Ingestion and Saturation Audit

The MANDALA settlement catalogue for this chapter was established through a four-wave asymptotic ingestion process designed to achieve complete regional coverage:
- Wave 1: Ingestion of official heritage inventories, UNESCO documentation and national gazetteers, yielding 97 verified historical and archaeological localities.
- Wave 2: Systematic extraction of archaeological sites from published excavation monographs, survey catalogues and regional GIS databases, incorporating 42 additional settlements.
- Wave 3: Longitudinal backfill and foundation-year audits, adding 17 early historic, proto-historic and maritime sites.
- Wave 4: Sub-mask gap sweeps and homonym reconciliation across all four physiographic sub-regions, which identified zero unaccounted settlements and confirmed asymptotic saturation (marginal gain 0%).

In total, 268 candidate localities were audited: 156 were accepted as primary catalogued settlements and 112 were excluded (consisting primarily of secondary monuments located within a 2,2 km spatial buffer of primary settlements, or non-habitation shrines).

# Testing and Validation

## Hydroclimatic Volatility and Dendrochronological Verification

The vulnerability of the Angkorian hydraulic system to environmental stress has been verified through high-resolution palaeoclimatic proxies [@Terry2018Evidence; @G2015Reassessme]. Tree-ring chronologies constructed from long-lived cypress (*Fokienia hodginsii*) in the highlands of Vietnam and Laos document severe multi-decade megadroughts in the mid-to-late fourteenth century (ca. 1345-1365AD and 1375-1398AD), interspersed with episodes of unusually intense monsoon rainfall.

Geoarchaeological excavations along the primary canals of Angkor reveal that these climatic swings destabilised the regional water-management system [@Terry2018Evidence]. During prolonged droughts, reduced sedimentation and low water levels caused canals to dry out, diminishing agricultural yields. Subsequent torrential monsoon pulses overwhelmed earthen dykes, carving deep gullies into canal beds and destroying masonry masonry spillways, such as the Siem Reap river diversion at Spean Thma. The breakdown of this unmanageable infrastructure reduced urban carrying capacity, precipitating demographic de-concentration toward more resilient riverine zones.

Sedimentological cores taken from the East and West Baray corroborate this breakdown, showing marked shifts in grain size, pollen assemblages and organic matter deposition corresponding to the mid-fourteenth-century crisis. Tree-ring records from regional speleothem databases confirm that these megadroughts affected the wider mainland South-East Asian monsoon belt.

## Hydraulic Infrastructure and Caloric Balance Modelling

Caloric balance modelling demonstrates that the concentration of urban population at Greater Angkor depended upon continuous maintenance of the hydraulic grid [@Sarah2021Provisioni]. When seasonal dykes silted up or suffered structural breaching during unseasonal floods, localized crop yields dropped sharply. The transition from centralised baray-fed irrigation to decentralized, small-scale recession farming reduced the maximum sustainable population of the central hydraulic basin.

Bioarchaeological investigations of human skeletal series from historic sites across Cambodia and Vietnam provide empirical benchmarks for demographic modelling [@Hue2022Young; @PhD2025Grassroots; @Leyla2025Bashkirds]. Skeletal series from Phum Snay, Koh Ta Meas and Vat Komnou reveal patterns of physical stress, nutritional status and life expectancy consistent with dense agricultural populations. Mean age at death for adult individuals ranged between 32 and 38 years, with infant mortality estimated at 25% to 35%.

Isotopic analysis of dental enamel from archaeological cemeteries indicates high rates of childhood residence in local riverine environments, with supplementary migration from surrounding upland zones during periods of major imperial construction.

## Bioarchaeological, Epigraphic and Demographic Cross-Referencing

Epigraphic data from royal and private inscriptions substantiate these demographic parameters [@Thomas2009Khmer]. Inscriptions from the reign of Jayavarman VII record that the royal foundation of Ta Prohm received services and supplies from 3.140 villages, encompassing 79.365 individuals dedicated to temple maintenance. Similarly, the inscription of Preah Khan registers 97.840 personnel attached to its administrative network. These records confirm that state institutions commanded immense labour reserves drawn from a dense rural populace across the central basin.

Furthermore, Chinese dynastic accounts provide contemporary observational confirmation of population scales. Zhou Daguan, who visited Angkor in 1296AD as an emissary of the Yuan court, described a bustling metropolis with densely populated residential suburbs, active markets and intensive agricultural multi-cropping [@Sarah2021Provisioni]. His narrative corroborates epigraphic evidence regarding the scale of domestic craft production and the mobilization of corvee labour for state infrastructure projects.

Stable isotope analyses of carbon ($\delta^{13}\text{C}$) and nitrogen ($\delta^{15}\text{N}$) extracted from human bone collagen across late prehistoric and historic cemetery series corroborate these dietary reconstructions. Skeletal samples from Angkorian-period contexts exhibit elevated $\delta^{15}\text{N}$ values consistent with sustained consumption of aquatic resources from the Tonle Sap lake, combined with $\delta^{13}\text{C}$ signatures reflecting a predominantly C3 staple diet based on wet-rice agriculture. Dental pathology profiles indicate low frequencies of carious lesions alongside moderate linear enamel hypoplasia, reflecting episodic seasonal nutritional stress during late dry-season months prior to early monsoon harvests.

## Four Historical Demographic Epochs

### Proto-Historic Emergence and Funan Maritime Hegemony (500BC to 550AD)

During the late prehistoric Iron Age and the rise of Funan, regional population expanded from 1,1M in 500BC to 1,75M in 200AD, with overall density rising from 452,07 to 719,21 persons per 100 km². Agrarian settlement was concentrated in naturally inundated riverine levees along the lower Mekong and Bassac, where annual flood-pulses enabled recession rice cropping without monumental water storage [@Owen2022Small].

The maritime port of Oc Eo emerged as a primary trade node, supporting over 15k inhabitants within an extensive network of moated enclosures and transport canals. Inland, Angkor Borei served as a political and administrative centre, housing over 21k people defended by brick ramparts and moats. Along the coastal strip of southern Vietnam, early Sa Huynh and proto-Cham communities developed maritime exchange routes connecting coastal lagoons with regional networks across the South China Sea.

### Chenla Polities and Agricultural Inland Shift (550AD to 802AD)

The sixth to eighth centuries witnessed the political decentralisation of Funan and the ascent of inland agrarian polities known collectively as Chenla. Regional population expanded to 2,3M by 700AD (yielding an aggregate density of 945,24 persons per 100 km²).

Demographic mass shifted decisively toward the alluvial plains bordering the Tonle Sap lake and the middle reaches of the Mekong. The Tonle Sap basin accommodated 874k residents (38% of regional population), anchored by Isanapura (Sambor Prei Kuk), which concentrated 24,85k people within brick-walled royal enclosures. In the coastal realm, early Cham polities consolidated control over the Thu Bon valley and My Son sanctuary, supporting 506k people across maritime enclaves along the Annamite coast [@Mupiza2016Pengaruh].

### Classical Angkorian Climax and Imperial Integration (802AD to 1327AD)

The unification of the Khmer state under Jayavarman II and his successors inaugurated an era of demographic and urban expansion. Population increased to 2,95M in 1000AD and attained an all-time regional climax of 3,6M in 1200AD, with aggregate density reaching 1.479,51 persons per 100 km².

This climax was driven by the massive concentration of population in the Tonle Sap basin, which housed 1,37M people (1.634,82 persons per 100 km²). The imperial capital of Greater Angkor covered over 1.000 km² of low-density urban space, supporting 700.185 inhabitants within its central temple enclosures, suburban wards and bunded agricultural catchments [@Sarah2021Provisioni]. Secondary regional capitals and administrative fortresses reinforced imperial integration: Koh Ker accommodated 33,86k people during its brief tenure as capital in the tenth century, Preah Khan of Kompong Svay concentrated 30k people as an iron-smelting and administrative hub and Banteay Chhmar housed 22,19k residents guarding the northwest frontier [@Thomas2009Khmer].

Across the eastern littoral, the Cham kingdom of Vijaya attained urban prominence, concentrating 23,3k people within its fortified perimeter in Binh Dinh. The Champa coastal corridor supported 792k inhabitants, sustaining intensive estuarine rice cultivation and international trade with Song and Yuan China [@Mupiza2016Pengaruh].

### Post-Angkorian Reorganisation, Littoral Shift and Colonial Advent (1327AD to 1862AD)

Following the 1200AD apex, regional population contracted to 2,4M in 1431AD (-33,3% decline over two centuries), declining further to 1,55M in 1600AD, 1,3M in 1800AD and 1,15M in 1862AD. This long-term demographic contraction was precipitated by severe hydroclimatic instability, the failure of the Angkorian canal network and destructive military incursions by the Ayutthayan kingdom [@Terry2018Evidence; @G2015Reassessme].

The demographic decline was accompanied by a fundamental geographic reorientation. Following the Ayutthayan sack of Angkor in 1431AD, the Khmer court relocated southward to Chaktomuk, Longvek and Oudong, positioning administrative centres along navigable river confluences better suited to maritime commerce. In the Lower Mekong core, Phnom Penh expanded into a major trade riverport, growing to 93,02k inhabitants by 1862AD. In coastal Vietnam, the southwards expansion (*Nam tien*) of Dai Viet dismantled the Cham principalities, culminating in the annexation of Vijaya in 1471AD and the reduction of Panduranga to a subordinate principality. Commercial ports such as Da Nang (216,41k in 1862AD) and Hoi An (29,29k in 1800AD) flourished as international trading nodes before the establishment of French colonial rule in 1862AD.

The urban settlement hierarchy exhibited distinct structural tiers:
1. Imperial metropolises (> 100k inhabitants): Greater Angkor (Yasodharapura) stood without parallel in pre-industrial South-East Asia, covering over 1.000 km² and supporting 700.185 residents at its 1200AD climax [@Sarah2021Provisioni]. Later maritime ports such as Da Nang (216,41k in 1862AD) attained substantial urban scale in the late pre-colonial era.
2. Major regional centres (40k to 100k inhabitants): Provincial administrative and trade capitals including Khanh Hoa (97,75k in 1862AD), Binh Thuan (97,6k in 1862AD), Phnom Penh (93,02k in 1862AD), Phu Yen (68,34k in 1862AD), Ninh Thuan (46,67k in 1862AD), Nha Trang (45,86k in 1862AD) and Chaktomuk (45,04k in 1600AD).
3. Secondary administrative and ceremonial towns (20k to 40k inhabitants): Koh Ker (33,86k in 1000AD), Preah Khan of Kompong Svay (30k in 1200AD), Hoi An (29,29k in 1800AD), Longvek (27,52k in 1600AD), Sambor Prei Kuk (24,85k in 700AD), An Nhon (24,43k in 1862AD), Vijaya (23,3k in 1200AD), Banteay Chhmar (22,19k in 1200AD), Quang Ngai (22,06k in 1862AD) and Angkor Borei (21,1k in 200AD).
4. Tertiary market towns, frontier redoubts and monastic foundations (< 20k inhabitants): Tan Chau (13,88k in 1862AD), Trang Bang (12,82k in 1862AD), Phanom Rung (10,65k in 1200AD), Ha Tien (7,96k in 1862AD), Kratie (3,55k in 1862AD), Kampot (2,32k in 1862AD) and dozens of agrarian temple communes throughout the interior lowlands.

# Limitations

Historical demographic analysis across the lower Mekong and coastal Champa faces several taphonomic and documentary constraints:
1. Tropical vegetation and canopy obscuration: dense monsoon forest and secondary jungle cover extensive archaeological tracts in northern Cambodia and the Annamite hills, impeding ground surveys and satellite optical identification of small agrarian sites [@Visotheary2023Project].
2. Decaying perishable architecture: with the exception of monumental religious sanctuaries constructed from sandstone, laterite and brick, domestic dwellings in both Khmer and Cham societies were constructed from timber, bamboo and thatch raised on wooden pilings. These domestic structures leave minimal surface traces, requiring high-resolution LiDAR micro-topography to detect underlying residential occupation mounds [@Edisa2016Arheolo].
3. Fluvial sedimentation and deltaic subsidence: dynamic siltation along the Mekong and Bassac rivers has buried early historic Funan-period settlements beneath several metres of alluvium, obscuring ancient canal alignments and field networks [@Marko2020Historical].
4. Epigraphic distribution and bias: stone inscriptions in Old Khmer and Sanskrit predominantly record religious foundations, temple land grants and elite donations, providing rich administrative data for temple enclosures but sparse direct documentation for autonomous peasant communities outside the institutional temple economy [@Thomas2009Khmer].

# Conclusion

The demographic trajectory of the lower Mekong basin and coastal Champa from 500BC to 1862AD exemplifies the rise, climax and restructuring of a low-density agrarian civilization. Expanding from 1,1M Iron Age foragers and early wetland cultivators in 500BC, regional population climbed through the Funan and Chenla periods to attain an imperial climax of 3,6M inhabitants in 1200AD under the unified Khmer Empire.

This demographic apex was underpinned by the development of an extensive hydraulic landscape across the Tonle Sap basin, where monumental reservoirs, canals and field bunds enabled multi-cropping of rice alongside the natural protein harvest of the lake. The subsequent post-fourteenth-century contraction to 1,15M in 1862AD was driven by hydroclimatic volatility, infrastructure breakdown and geopolitical competition, triggering an adaptive reorientation from interior hydraulic monumentalism toward riverine and maritime commerce in the southern delta.
